title: Jews in the Islamic world
hookLine: Baghdad, Cairo, Kairouan: long periods of flourishing, and times of hardship

cards: Kitab. It's the Arabic word for a book.

Saadia's great work of philosophy has it in its Arabic title, and it shows up in a phrase the Qur'an uses for Jews and Christians: ahl al-kitab, the people of the book, or as one old translation puts it, the People of the Scripture.
In the copies of Saadia's book that came down to us, kitab is spelled in Hebrew letters. Arabic words, Hebrew script: that way of writing is called Judeo-Arabic, a small window into a very big world.
For centuries, from Baghdad to Cairo to Kairouan, Jewish life unfolded in lands ruled by Muslims, and in Arabic.

teach.b: The academies we've been following, Sura and Pumbedita, came to sit in a world governed by Muslim rulers, whose capital was Baghdad.
Under Islamic law, Jews and Christians were usually treated as protected peoples, called dhimmi. They could keep their faith, their courts and their houses of worship.
They also paid a special tax and lived under limits, and how those limits felt depended a great deal on who was in power.

There were long stretches of flourishing. Jews worked as merchants, doctors, scholars and officials. They wrote poetry, philosophy and Bible commentary in Arabic, and their letters crossed seas because trade routes did.
Jewish thinkers read Muslim philosophers and argued with them; ideas moved in both directions. That's the world Saadia wrote from.
There were also hard times. In Cairo, for a time, a caliph ordered synagogues and churches torn down, before the policy was reversed. Some rulers enforced humiliating rules.
Communities sometimes faced violence, and some had to flee.
Both are true, and the honest history keeps both: neither perfect harmony nor constant persecution fits what the records show.
Neighbors, business partners, rivals, sometimes victims, sometimes friends, living the long middle of history side by side, and writing it down in Arabic, in Hebrew letters.

how: Jewish communities with roots in North Africa, the Middle East and Yemen keep traditions, melodies and words from centuries of life in Arabic-speaking lands, and Judeo-Arabic texts are still studied.

games.why: that's Judeo-Arabic: the everyday language, in the familiar letters. Saadia's book has come down written this way too.

practice: Say one Judeo-Arabic word quietly a few times: kitab, a book, which can be spelled in Arabic letters or in Hebrew ones, the way Saadia's book spells it.
Let it open a picture: a woman in Kairouan writing to her brother, in Arabic in Hebrew letters, about a wedding, a sick child, the price of bread, two languages in one line.
Hold that picture without deciding what it means, and if you pray, you can remember the people of that world.
